question: Why do dogs need omega fatty acids in their diet?
answer: Dogs require both omega-6 and omega-3 fatty acids daily, and their bodies cannot produce these essential fatty acids on their own. A deficiency quickly leads to dry skin, coat abnormalities, reproductive issues, and a general failure to thrive. The problem with modern feeding is that the vast majority of commercial and highly processed dog foods are very high in omega-6 and extremely low in omega-3. The most beneficial omega 6-to-3 ratio for supporting a healthy inflammatory response is 5:1 or less — many processed kibbles on the shelf have ratios as high as 30:1. That severe imbalance is what makes daily omega-3 supplementation a foundational piece of canine health rather than an optional extra.

question: What is the ideal omega 6 to omega 3 ratio for a dog?
answer: 5:1 or less. That's the ratio that supports a healthy inflammatory response. The problem is that most commercial and highly processed dog foods sit nowhere near it — many kibbles on the shelf run as high as 30:1, because they're loaded with omega-6 from plant oils and poultry fat while carrying almost no omega-3. This is why you can't assume a complete food has covered it. If your dog eats processed food, daily omega-3 supplementation is what closes that gap.

question: Will omega-3 help my dog's itchy skin and allergies?
answer: Yes — this is one of the strongest uses. Omega-3s are highly effective at preventing and managing allergic skin disease, and they target the symptoms directly: dry skin, hair loss, constant scratching, paw chewing and itching. The mechanism is that they modulate inflammatory pathways rather than just coating the skin from outside. Give it daily and consistently, and give it with food containing healthy fats to maximise absorption. For dosing, standard health is 30 to 60 mg of EPA/DHA per pound of body weight.

question: Is krill oil better than fish oil for dogs?
answer: Yes, for two reasons: absorption and safety. Krill oil is significantly more bioavailable and more easily absorbed in the intestinal tract than standard fish oil, so you need a much lower dose for the same therapeutic benefit — about 500 mg of krill oil per 20 pounds of body weight daily, compared to upwards of 1,000 mg of standard fish oil per 20 pounds. On safety, krill sits very low on the food chain, so it has virtually no detectable toxins, whereas fish oils sourced from higher up the chain like salmon tend to concentrate mercury and PCBs in their fat. Krill also contains only moderate, safe levels of vitamin A, so there is no vitamin A toxicity risk.

question: How much krill oil should I give my dog?
answer: 500 milligrams of krill oil per 20 pounds of body weight, daily. That's an adequate therapeutic dose. For comparison, standard fish oil needs 1,000 milligrams per 20 pounds daily to reach equivalent therapeutic levels — you need twice as much because fish oil isn't absorbed as efficiently. So a 60 lb dog needs about 1,500 mg of krill oil, or about 3,000 mg of fish oil. Give it with food containing healthy fats, which markedly increases absorption.

question: How much fish oil does my dog need?
answer: 1,000 milligrams of fish oil per 20 pounds of body weight, daily. Measured as active EPA and DHA rather than total oil, standard health is 30 to 60 mg per pound of body weight. For a therapeutic dose targeting arthritis or active inflammation, it's 1,000 mg of oil per 10 pounds of body weight. Always give it with some food in the stomach, ideally food containing healthy fats such as safflower oil, which markedly increases absorption.

question: Can I use flaxseed oil instead of fish oil for my dog?
answer: Not as a replacement. Dogs lack the efficient biological pathways required to convert plant-based ALA — the omega-3 found in flaxseed, sesame and sunflower oils — into the active forms EPA and DHA. Because of that conversion bottleneck, a food or supplement listing flaxseed as its omega-3 source has not given your dog meaningful EPA or DHA. Marine sources that provide direct, pre-formed EPA and DHA — fish, krill, squid or algal oil — are far more biologically valuable for dogs. If you need a plant-based option because your dog can't tolerate marine sources, use Ahiflower oil rather than flax.

question: What is Ahiflower oil and why is it better than flaxseed?
answer: Ahiflower oil is the plant-based omega source that actually works for dogs, and it's the answer if your dog can't tolerate marine sources but you want something sustainable. Unlike flax, it contains SDA — stearidonic acid — which bypasses the conversion bottleneck that limits ALA. It converts to EPA four times better than the ALA in flaxseed. That single difference is why it's worth choosing over flax when a plant source is required.

question: What is algal oil and is it good for dogs?
answer: Algal oil is a highly sustainable, sea-based omega-3 source that is exceptionally heavy in DHA. It's sourced directly from the algae at the very bottom of the food chain — the same algae that fish eat to get their own omega-3 — which makes it highly direct, pure and free of accumulated toxins. Because it's DHA-dominant, it's the strongest choice where brain and eye health is the goal, which means puppies in development and seniors facing cognitive decline. It's also the option for owners who want to avoid fish entirely.

question: Is cod liver oil safe to give my dog for omega-3?
answer: No — do not use cod liver oil as a general omega-3 source. It's made from the LIVER of the fish, where vitamins are heavily concentrated, so using it for everyday omega-3 carries a high risk of vitamin A toxicity. The signs of vitamin A toxicity are serious: malaise, peeling skin, tremors, convulsions, paralysis, and even death. Salmon and krill oils contain safe, moderate levels of vitamin A and are the appropriate choices. If you want omega-3, use krill, algal oil, or a contaminant-tested fish oil — not cod liver oil.

question: How should I store my dog's fish oil?
answer: Fish oil is extremely fragile and oxidises rapidly when exposed to light, heat and air — and rancid oil is highly toxic, causing the very inflammation and bodily damage you're trying to treat. Store it in cool, dark conditions and refrigerate it once opened. Use dark glass or brushed aluminium packaging, never plastic, which can leach chemicals into the oil. Buy smaller bottles and use them up within 4 weeks of opening. If it ever develops a strong, foul fishy odour, it has gone bad and must be discarded — don't try to use it up.

question: How long does fish oil stay good after opening?
answer: Four weeks. That's the freshness window. Oils oxidise and become rancid quickly once exposed to light, heat and air, and rancid oil is highly toxic — it drives the inflammation and bodily damage you bought the supplement to fix. Practical rules: buy smaller bottles so you finish them inside the window, keep it in the refrigerator once opened, store in dark glass or brushed aluminium rather than plastic, and discard immediately if a strong fishy odour develops. A big economy-sized bottle is a false saving if half of it turns rancid before you use it.

question: Does my dog need to stop fish oil before surgery?
answer: Yes. Fish oil decreases platelet stickiness and delays clotting times, which makes it a modest blood thinner. It must be stopped 7 to 14 days prior to any scheduled surgery to prevent excess bleeding. This is a genuinely important one that owners routinely miss — tell your vet what supplements your dog is on before any procedure, including dental work. Green-lipped mussel doesn't carry the same requirement, which is one practical advantage it has over fish oil.

question: Green-lipped mussel or fish oil — which should I choose for my dog?
answer: Both offer excellent anti-inflammatory support, but they're used differently. Green-lipped mussel is heavily favoured in canine therapeutic formulations as a specialised joint and mobility aid, typically paired with deer antler velvet, chondroitin and ginseng to target heart health and severe mobility issues in senior dogs. It also sits low on the food chain, so virtually no toxins. Fish oil is a highly effective direct source of EPA and DHA for general systemic health, but it comes with strict requirements green-lipped mussel doesn't have: contamination risk from mercury and PCBs, rapid oxidation needing refrigeration and a 4-week window, and stopping 7 to 14 days before surgery. For a senior dog whose main issue is mobility, green-lipped mussel. For broad systemic anti-inflammatory support, marine oil — ideally krill.

question: Do omega-3s help senior dogs with cognitive decline or dementia?
answer: Yes — for senior dogs, omega-3s are crucial for brain health and cognition. They can markedly improve the signs of cognitive dysfunction, which is the canine equivalent of Alzheimer's: pacing, altered sleep patterns, barking at walls, and changed interactions with owners. DHA is the fraction doing most of that work, since it's a structural building block of brain and nerve membranes. That makes algal oil a particularly strong choice for an ageing dog, because it's exceptionally heavy in DHA. Standard dosing is 30 to 60 mg of EPA/DHA per pound of body weight daily.

question: Can omega-3 help my dog's arthritis and joint pain?
answer: Yes — omega-3s relieve joint pain and reduce inflammation in dogs suffering from arthritis. For joints specifically you want the therapeutic dose rather than the maintenance one: 1,000 mg of oil per 10 pounds of body weight, which is roughly double the standard health amount. Green-lipped mussel is the other strong option here and is heavily favoured in canine therapeutic joint formulations, often combined with chondroitin and deer antler velvet for senior dogs with severe mobility issues. Give it consistently and with fatty food to maximise absorption.

question: Do omega-3s help dogs with cancer?
answer: Omega-3s act as receptor agonists that decrease inflammatory responses, improve chemotherapy efficacy, and enhance the survival and quality of life of cancer patients. There's also a direct mechanism: DHA can be cytotoxic to cancer cells. Cancer cells growing in acidic microenvironments take in too much DHA and essentially engorge themselves to death. That combination — reducing the inflammation cancer feeds on, improving how well chemo works, and being directly deadly to the cells — is why omega-3 is a standard part of a supportive cancer protocol rather than an afterthought.

question: How do omega-3s help leaky gut in dogs?
answer: EPA and DHA, the active omega-3 workhorses, embed themselves directly into the cell walls of the gut. That reinforces the gut lining — think of it as tightening a mesh strainer — which prevents toxic substances from passing through into the bloodstream and causing leaky gut and the immune system imbalances that follow. It's a structural effect rather than a signalling one, which is why consistency matters: you're rebuilding cell membranes over weeks, not delivering a dose that acts today.

question: Are omega-3s good for a dog with pancreatitis or liver problems?
answer: Yes. Omega-3s normalise fat metabolism, which makes them highly beneficial for managing canine pancreatitis and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. They also lower high triglycerides, which is often part of the same picture. On the wider organ front, they support heart health by reducing systemic inflammation and decreasing the risk of dangerous arrhythmias, and they improve heart and kidney function. Given a dog with pancreatitis needs fat carefully managed overall, work the supplement into the total fat plan with your vet rather than adding it on top.

question: What is krill and why is it used in dog supplements?
answer: Krill is a marine source of omega-3 fatty acids that provides high levels of the active workhorse nutrients, EPA and DHA. What makes it valuable for dogs is its position very low on the food chain — it hasn't accumulated the heavy environmental pollutants that plague larger marine life, so it has virtually no detectable toxins. It's also more bioavailable than standard fish oil, meaning more of it is absorbed when given orally, so you need a smaller dose: 500 mg per 20 pounds of body weight daily versus 1,000 mg for fish oil. And unlike cod liver oil it carries only moderate, safe vitamin A levels, so there's no toxicity risk.

question: Should I worry about mercury and PCBs in my dog's fish oil?
answer: It's a real consideration. Many fish oils are sourced from fish higher up the food chain, like salmon, and those fish accumulate ocean toxins such as mercury and PCBs in their fat — which is exactly the part the oil is pressed from. Two ways to handle it: buy a supplement verified as tested for contaminants, or choose a source lower on the food chain. Krill is the obvious one, sitting so low that it has virtually no detectable toxins. Algal oil is lower still, coming straight from the algae at the bottom of the chain. Green-lipped mussel also sits low and is virtually toxin-free.

question: Should I give my dog omega-3 with food or on an empty stomach?
answer: Always with food. Give omega-3 supplements with some food in your dog's stomach, and specifically food that contains healthy fats — safflower oil is a good example. This markedly increases absorption. Omega-3s are fat-soluble, so giving them alongside dietary fat is what gets them across the gut wall efficiently. Giving an expensive krill or algal oil on an empty stomach wastes a meaningful share of what you paid for.

question: What's the difference between EPA and DHA for dogs?
answer: They're the two active workhorse omega-3s and they do different jobs. EPA is the anti-inflammatory one — it's what's doing the work for joints, skin, allergies and inflammatory disease. DHA is the structural one, a physical building block of brain, retina and nerve membranes, which is why it matters most for puppies in development and seniors facing cognitive decline. Both come pre-formed from marine sources: fish, krill, squid and algal oil. Algal oil is particularly DHA-heavy. Plant sources like flax provide ALA instead, which dogs convert to EPA and DHA very poorly, which is why marine sources are far more biologically valuable.

question: My dog eats kibble. Does he still need omega-3 supplements?
answer: Almost certainly yes, and kibble is exactly why. The vast majority of commercial and highly processed dog foods are very high in omega-6 and extremely low in omega-3. The healthy ratio is 5:1 or less; many kibbles run as high as 30:1. On top of the formulation problem, omega-3s are fragile and degrade under the heat of processing and during shelf storage, so whatever was in the bag at manufacture isn't necessarily what's in the bowl. Daily omega-3 supplementation is a foundational piece of canine health for a processed-food dog. Start at standard health dosing — 30 to 60 mg of EPA/DHA per pound of body weight — and give it with food.
